questions.scenario: An analyst finds ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together, correlation 0.9, and proposes banning ice cream to save lives.
questions.question: What is the flaw?
options: A correlation of 0.9 is too low to matter.
Correlation does not imply causation. A third variable, hot weather, drives both, so this is a confounded relationship.
Correlation always implies causation when it is above 0.8.
The two variables must be measured in the same units.
questions.explanation: A strong correlation only says the two move together, not that one causes the other. Here a confounder, temperature, raises both ice-cream sales and swimming (and thus drownings). Establishing causation needs an experiment or careful causal reasoning, not a correlation coefficient.
questions.misconception: A high correlation is not evidence of causation. Always ask whether a confounder could drive both variables.

questions.question: Why is the Pearson correlation coefficient often preferred over raw covariance for describing the strength of a linear relationship?
options: Covariance only works for categorical data.
It is standardized to the range minus 1 to 1, so its magnitude is comparable across datasets, unlike covariance whose scale depends on the units.
Pearson correlation detects any relationship, including non-linear ones.
questions.explanation: Covariance captures the direction of a linear relationship but its size depends on the variables' units, so you cannot compare it across datasets. Pearson correlation divides covariance by the product of the standard deviations, giving a unitless value in minus 1 to 1 that is directly comparable.
questions.misconception: Pearson correlation measures LINEAR association only. A strong non-linear relationship can show a near-zero coefficient.

questions.question: You want to see how a numerical variable differs across the categories of a categorical variable (for example, fare by passenger class).
options: Use a single histogram of the numerical variable only.
Use a grouped box plot or violin plot, comparing the numerical distribution within each category.
Correlation is the only valid tool.
Use a scatter plot of the category against itself.
questions.explanation: Comparing a numerical distribution across categories is the categorical-numerical case. A grouped box plot or violin plot shows center, spread, and outliers per category side by side, which a single pooled histogram would hide.
